title: Small Kitchen Details That Make a Big Difference
content:
You don't need a full renovation to make your kitchen feel warmer and more put-together — just a few thoughtful details.

Start with your countertop. A few brown storage jars grouped together add texture and keep everyday staples within reach. A wooden spatula stand nearby keeps tools tidy without hiding them away.

Color matters too. A bold green knife set or a matching set of coffee mugs on open shelving instantly feels more intentional than tucking everything in a drawer.

Don't forget what's underfoot — a warm-toned kitchen mat ties the whole space together and adds comfort while you cook.

Even the small essentials deserve attention. A nice butter dish, a clean salt and pepper set, or a simple tissue box cover are touched daily, so they're worth choosing well.

The trick is consistency: pick one or two tones (like green or brown) and repeat them across a few pieces. That's what makes a kitchen feel styled, not just stocked.

title: The Return of Warmth: Five Interior Design Trends Making a Comeback in 2026
content:
For much of the last decade, interior design was defined by clean lines, bright white walls, and minimal décor. Homes embraced open layouts, monochromatic palettes, and an emphasis on simplicity. While these ideas remain influential, 2026 is revealing a noticeable shift in how people want their homes to feel.

Design professionals are increasingly observing homeowners moving toward interiors that prioritize warmth, individuality, and comfort over perfection. Instead of chasing every viral aesthetic, people are choosing spaces that reflect their lifestyles, personal collections, and everyday routines. Recent design reports suggest that timeless materials, layered textures, and practical layouts are replacing trends that once focused primarily on visual minimalism.

Here are five interior design movements making a strong comeback this year.

##1. Rich, Earthy Colours Are Replacing All-White Interiors

White walls have long been considered a safe choice. They make spaces feel larger, brighter, and easier to decorate. However, designers are now seeing a growing preference for richer colour palettes that create a stronger sense of comfort.

Earth-inspired shades such as olive green, terracotta, deep ochre, warm taupe, chocolate brown, and muted burgundy are appearing across living rooms, kitchens, and bedrooms. Rather than overwhelming a space, these colours provide depth while maintaining a calm and welcoming atmosphere.

Paint manufacturers and interior designers alike have noted a renewed appreciation for colours drawn from nature. These shades pair especially well with natural materials like oak, walnut, limestone, and linen, helping interiors feel more grounded rather than overly polished.

The shift doesn't necessarily mean every wall needs a dramatic colour. Many homeowners are introducing these tones through feature walls, cabinetry, upholstery, rugs, or decorative accessories before committing to larger design changes.

##2. Minimalism Is Giving Way to Personality##

Minimalism remains an important design philosophy, but its interpretation is changing.

Instead of empty shelves and carefully staged rooms, homeowners are embracing interiors that showcase personal stories. Family heirlooms, vintage finds, handcrafted ceramics, travel souvenirs, framed artwork, and curated book collections are becoming essential design elements rather than clutter.

Designers often describe this approach as "collected rather than decorated." The objective isn't to fill every corner but to create spaces that feel authentic and lived-in.

This evolution also reflects a broader lifestyle shift. As more people continue working remotely or spending greater amounts of time at home, interiors are expected to provide emotional comfort alongside visual appeal. Homes are increasingly seen as places for self-expression rather than showrooms designed for photographs.

##3. Built-In Storage Is Becoming a Smart Investment##

Space efficiency has become one of the biggest priorities for homeowners, particularly in cities where living areas are becoming more compact.

As a result, built-in furniture is returning as both a functional and aesthetic solution.

Window benches with hidden storage, floor-to-ceiling bookshelves, custom entertainment units, integrated wardrobes, and built-in dining seating allow homeowners to maximize available space while maintaining clean visual lines.

Unlike standalone furniture, custom-built storage can be designed around the specific dimensions of a room, making awkward corners and unused alcoves far more practical.

Beyond functionality, built-ins also contribute to a more cohesive interior. Instead of individual pieces competing for attention, the room feels intentionally designed, with storage seamlessly integrated into the architecture.

Although custom installations often require a larger upfront investment, many homeowners view them as long-term improvements that enhance both daily living and property value.

##4. Layered Lighting Is Replacing Single Ceiling Fixtures##

Lighting is increasingly being treated as one of the most important elements of interior design rather than an afterthought.

Instead of relying on a single overhead light, designers recommend combining multiple lighting sources to create depth and flexibility.

This layered approach generally includes:

Ambient lighting for overall illumination.
Task lighting for reading, cooking, or working.
Accent lighting to highlight artwork, architectural details, or decorative features.

Wall sconces, pendant lights, floor lamps, under-cabinet lighting, and concealed LED strips are being used together to create interiors that adapt throughout the day.

Warm lighting, typically around 2700K–3000K, continues to dominate residential spaces because it produces a softer and more comfortable atmosphere than cooler, bluish light commonly found in commercial environments.

The growing popularity of smart lighting systems has also made it easier for homeowners to adjust brightness and colour temperature according to different activities and moods.

##5. Natural Materials Continue to Lead Interior Design##

Perhaps the most enduring trend of 2026 is the growing appreciation for authentic materials.

Wood, stone, linen, clay, rattan, jute, and handmade ceramics are increasingly replacing synthetic finishes and mass-produced decorative elements.

Rather than striving for perfect uniformity, designers are celebrating natural imperfections such as wood grain variations, textured stone surfaces, and handcrafted finishes. These details bring character into interiors while creating stronger visual connections with nature.

Sustainability also plays a role in this movement. Consumers are becoming more interested in investing in fewer, higher-quality pieces that age gracefully instead of replacing inexpensive furniture every few years.

This philosophy aligns with the broader concept of "quiet luxury," where craftsmanship, durability, and timeless design take precedence over highly recognizable trends.

Looking Ahead

Interior design trends rarely move in straight lines. While minimalism continues to influence modern homes, 2026 demonstrates that many homeowners are searching for something beyond simplicity.

Comfort, functionality, and individuality are becoming central to residential design. Rich colours, layered lighting, thoughtful storage, and natural materials are helping create homes that feel welcoming rather than overly curated.

The most successful interiors are not necessarily those that follow every new trend but those that balance timeless design principles with the unique needs of the people who live in them. As the year progresses, designers expect this emphasis on warmth and personal expression to continue shaping homes across a wide range of architectural styles.

title: Why Beautiful Furniture Can Still Make a Bad Room
content:
## Why Beautiful Furniture Can Still Make a Bad Room

Have you ever seen a piece of furniture that you absolutely loved, bought it, and then wondered why it somehow didn't look right in your home?

It happens more often than people think. A beautiful sofa can look great in a showroom. So can a coffee table, a rug, a lamp, or a piece of artwork. But put all of them together without considering how they relate to one another, and the room can start to feel strangely disconnected.

That's because a well-designed room isn't really a collection of beautiful objects. It's a collection of relationships between them.

## The Problem With Buying One Piece at a Time

Most of us don't furnish a room all at once. We buy a sofa first, find a coffee table a few months later, add a rug when we find a good one, and eventually pick up a lamp or some artwork because we like it.

There's nothing wrong with doing this. The problem is that every purchase is being judged on its own.

You might end up with a beautiful walnut table, a cool grey sofa, a brass lamp, and a colourful rug. Each piece works perfectly by itself, but together they may have completely different tones, proportions, or styles.

Good design isn't about finding pieces that look good individually. It's about finding pieces that make each other look better.

## It's Not About Everything Matching

This doesn't mean your furniture needs to come from the same collection or that everything has to match.

In fact, rooms can become much more interesting when different styles are mixed thoughtfully. A modern sofa can work beautifully with a vintage wooden table. A simple room can handle a bold piece of artwork. The trick is finding something that connects them — perhaps a similar colour, material, shape, proportion, or even just a shared sense of warmth.

Think of it like putting together an outfit. Your shoes, jacket, and trousers don't have to be identical. They just need to make sense together.

## Scale Matters More Than We Think

One of the easiest ways to make a room feel "off" is to get the scale wrong.

A coffee table might be beautiful but too small for the sofa. A rug might be gorgeous but too small for the seating area. A pendant light might look perfect online but completely disappear above a large dining table.

These are things that are difficult to understand from a product photograph alone. Furniture doesn't exist in isolation; it exists in a room.

Before asking whether you love a piece, it's worth asking whether its size and proportions make sense with what you already have.

## Colour and Material Need a Conversation

The same idea applies to colour and materials. A room doesn't need to follow a strict colour palette, but there should usually be some connection between the different elements.

- Maybe the warmth of an oak table is picked up again in a wooden shelf.
- Maybe the black metal of a floor lamp appears subtly in the furniture hardware.
- Maybe the muted green in a rug is repeated in a cushion or piece of artwork.

These small repetitions are what make a room feel cohesive without making it look like everything was bought from the same catalogue.

## And Sometimes, Less Really Is More

There's another part of interior design that is surprisingly difficult: knowing when to stop.

When you've found something beautiful, it can be tempting to find a place for it. But not every empty corner needs a chair, every wall needs artwork, or every shelf needs decoration.

A little breathing room can make the things you already love stand out more.

## A Room Is More Than Its Products

This is probably the biggest thing we believe at Urban Nest: interior design shouldn't feel like a shopping list.

You shouldn't have to buy a beautiful sofa, a beautiful table, a beautiful lamp, and hope that somehow they become a beautiful room.

The best interiors happen when the individual pieces are considered together — their colours, materials, proportions, lighting, and the way they interact with the space around them.

Because ultimately, the goal isn't to fill your home with beautiful things.

It's to create a home where those things belong together.

This article explores why thoughtful combinations matter more than simply buying things you like—and how small design decisions can make a space feel cohesive, intentional, and truly yours.

title: The 5 Decisions You Should Make Before Buying Any Furniture
content:
Buying furniture is surprisingly easy now. You can see something you like on Instagram, save it, find it online, and have it delivered to your home within days.

The difficult part isn't finding something beautiful.

It's knowing whether it belongs in your space.

Before buying your next sofa, table, chair, rug, or lamp, there are five decisions worth making first. They can save you from expensive mistakes and, more importantly, help you create a room that feels intentional rather than assembled piece by piece.

## 1. Decide How You Want the Room to Feel

Before thinking about furniture, think about the atmosphere you want.

Do you want the room to feel warm and relaxed? Bright and energetic? Calm and minimal? Rich and sophisticated? Natural and earthy?

This sounds simple, but it gives every decision that follows a direction.

A warm, relaxed living room might lead you toward softer fabrics, warm woods, earthy colours, and diffused lighting. A more contemporary space might call for cleaner shapes, stronger contrasts, and simpler materials.

Start with the feeling, not the product.

## 2. Measure the Room — Then Measure Again

A product can look perfect online and completely wrong once it arrives.

Before buying anything substantial, understand the space you're working with. Measure the length and width of the room, the height of the ceiling, the position of doors and windows, and the space you'll need to move around the furniture.

Don't forget the practical details either. Will the sofa actually fit through the doorway? Can cabinet doors open properly? Is there enough room to walk comfortably around the dining table?

Furniture isn't just about dimensions on a product page.

It's about how those dimensions interact with everything around them.

## 3. Choose a Colour and Material Direction

You don't need a perfectly strict colour palette, but you should have some idea of where you're going.

If you already have a walnut floor, for example, adding several completely different wood tones can make the room feel visually busy. Similarly, a cool grey sofa might need warmer materials and lighting around it to prevent the space from feeling cold.

Think about the materials you want to repeat throughout the room — perhaps wood, linen, stone, metal, or glass.

Repeating a few materials and colours creates subtle connections between pieces.

The room doesn't need to match. It needs to relate.

## 4. Think About the Pieces Together

This is where many furniture purchases go wrong.

Instead of asking, "Do I like this chair?", ask:

"What will this chair look like next to my sofa?"

Then think about the coffee table, rug, lighting, curtains, artwork, and everything else that will eventually share the room.

You don't need to buy everything at once. But you should have a rough idea of how the pieces will interact before committing to one of them.

A beautiful sofa can make a room better.

The right sofa, with the right rug, table, lighting, and proportions can make the whole room better.

## 5. Decide What You Actually Need

Finally, resist the urge to fill the room.

An empty corner isn't automatically a problem that needs furniture. A blank wall doesn't necessarily need artwork. And a large coffee table doesn't need to be surrounded by five decorative objects just because there is space for them.

Think about how you actually live.

Where do you sit? Where do you work? Where do you store things? Where does natural light enter? Where do people move through the room?

Good interiors aren't designed around empty spaces. They're designed around real life.

## Design First. Shop Second.

Furniture shopping often starts with the question:

"What should I buy?"

A better question is:

"What does my room need?"

Once you understand the mood, proportions, materials, layout, and function of the space, choosing individual products becomes much easier.

You stop buying things simply because you like them.

You start choosing things because they belong.

And that's ultimately what good interior design is about — not filling a room with beautiful products, but making thoughtful decisions that allow everything in it to work together.

title: Why Modern Wall Trims and Mouldings Are Making a Comeback
content:
A room can have beautiful furniture, colour, and lighting yet still feel unfinished. Increasingly, homeowners and designers are turning to a classic architectural detail to bring walls back into focus: modern wall trims and mouldings.

Once associated mainly with traditional interiors, mouldings are making a comeback in fresh, contemporary forms. Slim profiles, clean lines, geometric layouts, and minimalist panelling can add structure, depth, and character without requiring a major renovation.

## Turning Blank Walls Into Designed Features

Modern wall trims make walls feel like part of the interior design rather than simple backdrops. Framed panels, arches, linear details, and geometric patterns can create visual zones for:

* Artwork and mirrors
* Accent lighting
* Contrasting colours
* Decorative focal points
* Media units and furniture groupings

Even a modest amount of moulding can have a significant visual impact. A simple grid or a few carefully placed panels can transform a flat wall into a considered architectural feature.

## Why Mouldings Are Making a Comeback

The renewed popularity of mouldings reflects a wider interest in interiors that feel layered, personal, and architectural. Modern spaces can sometimes appear overly plain, particularly when they rely on large expanses of painted walls. Trims introduce detail and craftsmanship while still working with contemporary furniture and finishes.

Today’s mouldings are also more versatile than traditional decorative styles. Minimal profiles can create a refined look, while bold geometric arrangements offer a more expressive, design-led finish. This makes them suitable for everything from compact apartments to open-plan homes.

## Adding Architectural Character

Wall trims can suggest decorative panelling, framed openings, or bespoke detailing without changing the structure of a room. This makes them especially useful in apartments and other spaces where extensive construction is impractical.

They can also help define different areas within an open-plan interior. A moulded feature wall behind a sofa, bed, dining table, or television can give the space a stronger sense of purpose and visual balance.

## Why Proportion Matters

A successful trim design depends on careful planning. Consider:

* The size and shape of each frame
* Spacing between panels
* Alignment with doors and windows
* The height at which the design begins
* The overall scale of the room
* The relationship between the moulding and nearby furniture

Well-planned proportions create balance and rhythm, while crowded or uneven layouts can make a wall feel unsettled. Modern moulding designs often rely on restraint, with generous spacing and clean, consistent lines.

## A Style for Every Interior

Modern wall trims and mouldings can suit many design styles:

* Traditional moulding adds elegance and heritage
* Slim profiles complement contemporary rooms
* Arches create softness and warmth
* Geometric designs make a modern statement
* Vertical trims can emphasise ceiling height
* Horizontal details can make a room feel wider

Matching the trim to the wall creates a subtle, seamless finish, while contrasting colours make the details stand out. Painting the moulding and wall in the same shade is a popular modern approach, allowing shadows and texture to create interest without introducing strong contrast.

Lighting can further enhance the moulding through highlights and shadows. Wall lights, concealed LED strips, and directional spotlights can emphasise the depth of the design and make the feature feel more architectural.

## When Less Is More

The best modern trim designs do not always demand attention. They can add texture, frame artwork, and make a room feel more considered without overwhelming the space.

A simple, well-placed moulding design can introduce symmetry, depth, and visual interest. As mouldings make their comeback, their appeal lies in their ability to combine timeless architectural character with a clean, contemporary finish.

Sometimes, all a plain wall needs is a little structure to give the entire room a more cohesive and finished identity.

title: Living in Harmony: Sanatani Inspiration for the Spaces We Call Home
content:
### A Sanatani way of looking at the spaces around us

There is a thought deeply woven into Sanatani philosophy: **the world around us is not separate from us.**

We are shaped by what we consume, what we listen to, what we see, what we surround ourselves with — and perhaps, most quietly of all, by the spaces we inhabit every day.

A home is therefore more than four walls and a roof.

It is where we wake up, where we gather, where we rest, where we think, where we celebrate and where we become, little by little, who we are.

Long before *interior design* became an industry, Indian thought had a language for understanding the relationship between human beings, nature and space.

Not as decoration.

As harmony.

---

## *Yatha pinde tatha brahmande.*

**As is the individual, so is the universe.**

One of the recurring ideas across Sanatani thought is that the human being and the cosmos are not entirely separate. The same elements that exist in the world around us exist within us.

Earth. Water. Fire. Air. Space.

This way of seeing the world changes how we might think about a room.

A space isn't simply something we fill with objects. It has light, proportion, movement, texture, openness and stillness. It can feel heavy or light. Restless or peaceful. Cold or welcoming.

And while modern design might describe these things through colour theory, ergonomics or spatial psychology, the older Indian imagination approached the relationship more holistically.

**The space around you participates in the experience of being you.**

Perhaps that is why a beautiful home has never really been about having beautiful things.

It has been about creating a beautiful way of living.

---

## *Sthāna* — there is meaning in where we are

The Sanskrit idea of *sthāna* refers to place, position or location.

But a place, in the Indian imagination, was rarely just a physical coordinate.

A temple had a particular spatial logic because it was meant to facilitate a particular state of being.

A courtyard brought light, air and people together.

A *diya* transformed a corner of a home not because it was an expensive object, but because of what its presence represented.

The threshold mattered.

The centre mattered.

The direction of the morning light mattered.

There was an understanding that **different spaces invite different states of mind.**

And perhaps we intuitively understand this even today.

We create a quiet corner to read.

We gather around a dining table.

We keep photographs of people we love where we can see them.

We put flowers in a room because somehow, the room feels different when something living is in it.

None of this is accidental.

We are constantly arranging our surroundings to create the lives we want to live.

---

## Beauty was never merely ornamental

There is another distinctly Indian idea worth remembering: **beauty and meaning were never necessarily opposites.**

The Sanskrit word *sundaram* points towards beauty, but Indian aesthetics traditionally went much deeper than simply making something visually pleasing.

The arts were capable of evoking *rasa* — a felt experience, an emotional flavour.

Perhaps this gives us another way to think about interiors.

A room can have a *rasa*.

Some spaces energise us.

Some calm us.

Some make us nostalgic.

Some make us want to linger.

Some simply make us feel at home.

So when we choose a sculpture, a lamp, a painting or even an empty patch of wall, we are not only choosing how the room looks.

We are choosing, consciously or otherwise, **how we want the room to feel.**

And that feeling becomes part of our everyday life.

---

## *Prakriti* was never meant to be far away

Modern life has created a strange separation.

We spend much of our time surrounded by things made by humans, under artificial light, inside constructed environments — and then seek nature as an escape.

The Sanatani worldview offers a different relationship with *prakriti*.

Nature isn't merely somewhere we visit.

**We are part of it.**

This is why traditional Indian spaces so often embraced courtyards, water, sunlight, plants, natural materials, breeze and the changing rhythms of the day.

The purpose wasn't necessarily to make a room look “natural.”

It was to allow the human experience to remain connected to the larger world.

A window isn't just an architectural opening.

It is a relationship with light.

A plant isn't just décor.

It is a reminder of life.

A stone object carries something different from plastic.

Wood ages.

Metal changes.

Clay remembers the hand that shaped it.

Perhaps good interiors don't need to imitate nature.

They simply need to **leave room for nature to be present.**

---

## The home as an extension of the self

There is something revealing about the things we choose to keep around us.

A home slowly becomes a collection of our memories, our aspirations, our tastes and our stories.

The books we keep.

The photographs we frame.

The objects we inherited.

The things we brought back from somewhere we loved.

The sculpture we couldn't stop thinking about.

The chair everyone fights over.

The little corner nobody planned but somehow became everyone's favourite.

These things make a house personal.

And perhaps that is the most beautiful lesson we can take from the Sanatani view of space:

**A meaningful life does not happen somewhere outside the objects and spaces around us.**

It happens within them.

---

## So, what makes a space good?

Maybe it isn't the number of things inside it.

Maybe it isn't whether everything matches.

Maybe it isn't even whether the room follows a particular style.

Perhaps a good space is one that allows you to become more fully yourself.

A space that gives you room to breathe.

A space that welcomes people.

A space that remembers.

A space that makes ordinary moments feel a little less ordinary.

A space that brings some balance between *prakriti* and *purusha*, between movement and stillness, between what we need and what we simply love.

The modern world has given us countless ways to decorate our homes.

The Sanatani tradition offers something slightly different.

**A way to think about why we create them.**

Because ultimately, we don't decorate spaces simply to look at them.

**We live inside them.**

And perhaps the spaces we choose to live in quietly become a part of the life we choose to live.

### Urban Nest

**Just The Right Feel.**

title: The Difference Between Decorating and Designing
content:
There’s a difference between a home that is filled with beautiful things and a home that feels beautifully considered.

The first is decorating.

The second is designing.

The distinction may sound subtle, but it changes the way we think about our spaces. Decorating often begins with a question: What should I add? Designing begins somewhere else: What should this space feel like?

A well-designed home isn't necessarily larger, more expensive, or filled with designer furniture. In fact, some of the most inviting spaces are built around relatively simple choices — the right proportions, a restrained palette, natural textures, thoughtful lighting, and objects that have a reason to be there.

Decorating adds. Designing decides.

Decorating is often about the visible layer of a home: cushions, artwork, vases, rugs, candles, trays and decorative objects. These things can instantly change a room, and there is absolutely nothing wrong with that.

But when every empty surface becomes an invitation to add something, a room can quickly become crowded.

Design asks a different question.

Instead of asking what can be added, it asks what should remain.

Where should the eye rest?
Which objects deserve attention?
How should one material interact with another?
Does the room feel balanced?
Is there enough empty space?

Sometimes the best design decision is not adding another beautiful object. It's leaving a little room around the ones already there.

A beautiful room isn't about matching everything

One of the easiest ways to decorate a home is to buy everything as a set.

The same colour. The same material. The same finish.

It feels safe, but it can also make a room feel predictable.

Good design is more interested in relationship than repetition.

A warm wooden surface might sit alongside stone. Soft textiles can contrast with harder finishes. A muted palette can be given depth through different textures rather than a dozen different colours.

The individual pieces don't need to be identical. They simply need to belong together.

This is why a collection of carefully chosen objects can feel more cohesive than a room full of individually beautiful purchases.

Proportion matters more than price

A ₹500 object can look completely at home in a beautifully designed space, while a much more expensive piece can feel out of place.

Why?

Often, it's proportion.

A small object sitting alone on a large surface may disappear. Several large objects crowded onto a narrow shelf can feel overwhelming. A rug that's too small can make an entire living room feel disconnected.

Design is largely about understanding these relationships.

Before asking “Is this beautiful?”, it can be useful to ask:

“Is this the right size, shape and scale for this space?”

It's a surprisingly powerful question.

The details we interact with every day matter

We tend to think about design in terms of the big decisions — the sofa, the dining table, the flooring, the kitchen cabinets.

But we interact with dozens of smaller objects every single day.

The soap dispenser beside the sink.
The jar on the kitchen counter.
The rug beneath our feet.
The tray that gathers the things we carry into a room.
The object sitting quietly on a bedside table.

These aren't insignificant simply because they're small.

In many ways, they're what make a home feel lived in and intentional.

A beautiful home isn't created only by the things we notice from across the room. It's created by the details we encounter when we're actually living in it.

Design is about creating a feeling

Perhaps the biggest difference between decorating and designing is that decorating tends to focus on appearance, while design considers experience.

What should it feel like to walk into the room in the morning?

Should the bedroom feel quiet and restful?

Should the kitchen feel organised and effortless?

Should the living room encourage conversation?

Should the bathroom feel clean, calm and unhurried?

Once you know the feeling you're trying to create, your choices become much easier.

You don't need to chase every new trend. You don't need to buy something simply because it looks good in someone else's home.

You can choose based on whether it belongs in your home.

Curate, don't accumulate

This might be the simplest way to think about it.

Decorating is collecting things you like.
Designing is curating the things you keep.

That doesn't mean a home should be minimalist or empty. A home should have personality. It should show the people who live there.

But personality doesn't require clutter.

The goal isn't to have fewer things for the sake of having fewer things. It's to have things that work together — objects that are useful, beautiful, meaningful, or simply make everyday life a little better.

Over time, these choices create something much more personal than a particular interior style.

They create a home.

The home should feel like you

There will always be another trend, another colour palette, another piece of furniture that looks perfect somewhere else.

But a well-designed home doesn't need to follow every trend.

It needs to make sense for the people who live in it.

That's ultimately what separates decorating from designing.

Decorating asks, “What looks good here?”

Design asks, “What belongs here?”

And sometimes, that small shift in thinking is all it takes to start seeing your home differently.

Because a beautiful home isn't built by filling every corner.

It's built by choosing what deserves to be there.
excerpt: Decorating fills a space. Designing gives it a sense of purpose. Here's why the difference matters when creating a home that feels truly yours.
